snapshot.title: Laboratory geometry: a restricted inertial chart, its spatial slices and fixed-time fields
snapshot.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. (d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer field is defined here.
snapshot.strategy: A construction definition with elementary verifications. The inertial chart $x$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] is a bijection, so its restriction to the set of events whose chart coordinates lie in $cI\times\Omega$ has image $cI\times\Omega$; composing with the bijection $cI\times\Omega\to I\times\Omega$, $(ct,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ (bijective because $c>0$) gives the bijection $\Phi$. Each slice $U_t$ is $\Phi^{-1}(\{t\}\times\Omega)$, on which $r$ restricts to a bijection onto $\Omega$. The claims about $n$, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $\delta$ and the orientation are exactly the content of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]; the $C^k$ notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and the two kinds of partial derivative are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] applied to the product coordinates. Clause (d) records conventions only: the frame dependence of $r,\delta$ and slices is stated rather than hidden, and no Galilean or observer-congruence claim is made. Nothing here uses a theorem of the framework, and the laboratory region may be a proper subset of $A$; no global chart of $A$ other than the given inertial chart is asserted.

snapshot.title: Frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pairs and their real-field encoding
snapshot.reference: scaffold-added necessary formulation prerequisite for the vector PEC scattering theorem (see research/physics-em-sr-40-2026-10-08-batch-40.notes.md)
snapshot.statement: Let $\omega>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set, and let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the vacuum constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Phasor encoding] For every pair of $C^\infty$ maps $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) define the **associated real fields** $$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\qquad((x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R),$$ componentwise, with the complex exponential and real part of [[def-complex-exponential]] and [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; this is the encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] specialized from plane-wave amplitudes to a general $C^\infty$ amplitude, and the complex fields are not themselves physical fields. (b) [Source-free class] The pair $(\widetilde E,\widetilde B)$ is called a **frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on $D$** when it is $C^\infty$ and satisfies, on $D$, $$\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega\varepsilon_0\mu_0\widetilde E=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E,$$ with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied componentwise to the complex fields. The word 'source-free' records that the displayed equations carry no charge or current term; the associated real fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]], $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $T:=2\pi/\omega$ the period. (c) [Status and scope] This item fixes the encoding, the four phasor equations and the terminology only. It asserts no equation for the associated real fields, no outgoing or boundary condition, no existence or uniqueness statement, no energy or flux reading and no empirical content. In particular the deduction that the associated real fields satisfy the smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations with zero sources is not part of this definition; for the pairs used on this page it is established by the exterior-scattering theorem recorded later on this page. Only $C^\infty$ pairs on an open set are defined, so no boundary trace, weak or distributional class is introduced here.
snapshot.strategy: This is a definition contract assembled from earlier items; well-definedness is discharged by the cited suppliers. (i) The encoding (a) is the real-part-of-complex-amplitude convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] with a general $C^\infty$ spatial amplitude; the componentwise real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] are total on $\mathbb C^3$, so the associated real fields are defined for every $C^\infty$ pair, with no equation assumed. (ii) The class (b) is cut out by four equations on the open set $D$: the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] act componentwise on the $C^\infty$ complex fields, and the two constants satisfy $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=c^{-2}$ by [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the displayed third and fourth equations use only complex scalar multiplication, so the class is well-defined without any choice principle. (iii) The physical reading of the associated real fields as an electric and a magnetic field uses [[def-em-fields]]; the units of $\widetilde E$ are V$\,$m$^{-1}$ and those of $\widetilde B$ are T, inherited from that definition. (iv) Clause (c) records exactly what is not asserted; in particular the complex Maxwell-to-real-Maxwell deduction is deliberately left to a consumer, because a definition must not assert the field equations of its associated real fields.

snapshot.title: Real plane-wave fields encoded by complex amplitudes
snapshot.statement: Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular frequency $\omega>0$ ($k$ carries $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$ the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), and fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$ componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$, $\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**, $\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the **angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**, and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then: (a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; on the whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. (b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through $\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$. (c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave **nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the magnetic field alone determines $b$, because $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$ (evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$). (d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no energy claim and no polarisation classification; those are the content of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realisation or measurement is claimed.
snapshot.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition. The domain, regularity and the identity of the real fields are those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] read on the whole-space laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; the field notion, class and units are those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. The phase convention $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$ (decreasing in $t$) is fixed here and used by every later item of the page: it is the convention in which the amplitude equations hold with the signs written in the cited treatments. The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of $w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$, recorded because later items speak of a 'nonzero wave'. No field equation or physical interpretation is introduced.
snapshot.physical_scope: Ideal whole-space classical plane-wave fields with wavevector $k\ne0$, angular frequency $\omega>0$, complex amplitudes in $\mathbb C^3$ and the SI units of the framework, defined on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. No source, boundary, decay, finite-energy or empirical content is asserted.

snapshot.title: Framework-local SI units, the vacuum constants and the exact/measured status of their values
snapshot.statement: Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted (the pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate/uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value); the electric constant is defined within the framework by $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of [[def-em-sources]] carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ carries kg m s$^{-1}$ ([[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]); field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI, they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]].
snapshot.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalisation $x^0=ct$, the unit of each quantity used in this framework, the exact SI defining values of $c$ and $e$ and the measured status of $\mu_0$. The exact values $c=299\,792\,458$ m/s and $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and the statements that the new definition of the ampere fixes $e$ rather than $\mu_0$, that $\mu_0$ must now be determined experimentally, and that $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$ remains exact, are taken from the SI brochure's defining-constants table and its ampere section. The framework's definition of $\varepsilon_0$ by $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ is a definition consistent with that exact relation; the uncertainty carried by $\varepsilon_0$ is recorded rather than hidden. The dimensional checks of the framework's equations and couplings are developed on the companion examples page of this pair. No exact or current measured numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted and no experiment is claimed. The historical nominal and adoption uncertainty are explicitly source context, not a substitution for the current experimentally determined constant.

## Definition

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

## Remarks

- **Scope: the concrete form only.** What is defined above is the Euclidean inner
  product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and nothing more. The general theory of inner
  product spaces — abstract inner products, orthonormal bases, Gram-Schmidt,
  orthogonal projection and orthogonal complements of arbitrary subspaces — is
  planned for a page of this library that comes **earlier in the plan order** and
  is not yet built. No item on this page claims anything about abstract inner
  product spaces, and no item on this page introduces the general notion.

- **The standard basis and coordinates.** For $i < n$ the standard unit vector
  $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ has $e_i(i) = 1$ and $e_i(j) = 0$ for $j \ne i$
  ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). Then $\langle x, e_i\rangle = x_i$: the list
  $k \mapsto x_k (e_i)_k$ vanishes except at $k = i$, where its value is $x_i$,
  and a list vanishing off one index sums to its value there
  ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 3, splitting the range at $i$). So the
  coordinates of $x$ are recovered by testing against the standard basis, which
  is the form used repeatedly below.

- **Powers here are integer powers.** $x_k^{2}$ means the integer power of
  [[def-integer-power]], and $\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} = \langle x,x\rangle$ by
  [[thm-of-square-roots]] and [[lem-power-laws]].

## Definition

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Because
$|\nu|$ is a measure ([[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]]), define
$$L^1(\nu):=L^1(|\nu|)$$
using the published meaning of $L^1$ from [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]].

If $f\in L^1(\nu)$, choose complex simple functions $s_n$ as in
[[thm-l-one-functions-admit-dominated-complex-simple-approximations]] with
$\int |f-s_n|\,d|\nu|\to0$. The simple-integral bound
[[prop-simple-integrals-are-bounded-by-total-variation]] makes
$(\int s_n\,d\nu)$ a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb C$, and its limit is
independent of the chosen approximating sequence. Define
$$\int f\,d\nu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int s_n\,d\nu.$$

For a measurable set $E\in\mathcal A$, define
$$\int_E f\,d\nu:=\int f\mathbf 1_E\,d\nu.$$

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

## Remarks

- **The vector case is componentwise by convention, and the convention is stated because sources leave it implicit.** Nothing forces a single reading of $\Delta$ on a field; the componentwise one is the one that makes the curl-of-a-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] true as written, and it is the reading in force everywhere on this page.

- **Why $C^2$ and not $C^1$.** Forming $\nabla f$ consumes one degree of differentiability, so $\operatorname{div}\nabla f$ needs $\nabla f$ to be $C^1$; that is exactly $f$ being $C^2$. Nothing here interchanges two partial derivatives, so no appeal to a mixed-partials theorem is made in the definition itself, and $\Delta f$ is defined by the displayed sum in the fixed order $\partial_i\partial_i$.

- **The planar equation.** For $n=2$ the condition $\Delta f=0$ reads $\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf=0$. That is the equation written out in [[thm-c2-holomorphic-components-are-harmonic]] for the real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function; a reader meeting the word "harmonic" in either place is meeting one notion.

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

## Definition

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

## Definition

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

## Statement

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $z=a+bi$ and $w=u+vi$.

[F1] Complex numbers have unique real coordinates and the coordinate addition and multiplication formulas ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

[F2] Conjugation and modulus are defined by $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$ and $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

[F3] The real numbers are a complete ordered field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), and every nonnegative element of a complete ordered field has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F4] For nonnegative elements $r,s$ of an ordered field, $r\le s$ if and only if $r^2\le s^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[F5] The square of every nonzero element of an ordered field is positive ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Coordinate expansion using [F1] and [F2] proves the two homomorphism laws, that conjugation fixes every real number, and that applying it twice is the identity. Thus conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Direct multiplication gives $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Lagrange's identity gives $$ (a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)-(au+bv)^2=(av-bu)^2\ge0. $$ The final inequality follows from [F5], with the zero case included. [F5, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] and [F3], $|z|\ge0$. If $z=0$, then $|z|=0$; conversely, $|z|=0$ makes $a^2+b^2=0$, and [F5] forces $a=b=0$. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

3.1 Apply step 1.2 to $zw$ and use step 1.1: $|zw|^2=(zw)\overline{zw}=(z\overline z)(w\overline w) =|z|^2|w|^2$. Both sides of $|zw|=|z||w|$ are nonnegative, so uniqueness in [F3] proves multiplicativity. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 Hence $au+bv\le |z||w|$: if $au+bv\le0$ this follows from $|z||w|\ge0$; otherwise both quantities are nonnegative, step 1.3 and [F4] give the inequality after squaring. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.1 Expanding with [F1] and [F2], then using step 3.2, gives $$ |z+w|^2=a^2+b^2+u^2+v^2+2(au+bv) \le (|z|+|w|)^2. $$ [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Both sides of $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$ are nonnegative, so [F4] turns the squared inequality in step 4.1 into the triangle inequality. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open set $U$, the $C^1$ maps $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$, the $C^1$ scalar $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and the reals $a,b$ of the Statement.

[F1] The divergence of a $C^1$ field $F$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, and for $n=3$ its curl is $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]).

[F2] For scalar-valued $f$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, the gradient is $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

[F3] For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F4] For $x,y\in\mathbb R^m$, $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<m}x_ky_k$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F5] A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[L1] For real functions of one real variable differentiable at a point, $f+g$ is differentiable there with $(f+g)'=f'+g'$, $\alpha f$ is differentiable there with $(\alpha f)'=\alpha f'$, and $fg$ is differentiable there with $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 A partial derivative $\partial_j$ at a point $p$ is the ordinary one-variable derivative at $0$ of $t\mapsto(\,\cdot\,)(p+te_j)$, so [L1] applies to it verbatim: for scalar $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $U$ and reals $a,b$ one has $\partial_j(au+bv)=a\,\partial_ju+b\,\partial_jv$ and $\partial_j(uv)=(\partial_ju)v+u\,\partial_jv$ pointwise on $U$, and the right-hand sides are continuous, so $au+bv$ and $uv$ are again $C^1$. [given, L1, F5]

1.2 Applying 1.1 componentwise, $aF+bG$ and $fF$ have $C^1$ components, hence are $C^1$ by [F5]; so all four expressions in the Statement are defined. [given, L1, F5]

2.1 By [F1], $\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i(aF_i+bG_i)$, and step 1.1 rewrites each summand as $a\,\partial_iF_i+b\,\partial_iG_i$; summing gives $a\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i+b\sum_{i<n}\partial_iG_i=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.2 By [F1], the first coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)$ is $\partial_y(aF_z+bG_z)-\partial_z(aF_y+bG_y)$, which step 1.1 rewrites as $a(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y)+b(\partial_yG_z-\partial_zG_y)$; the second coordinate is $\partial_z(aF_x+bG_x)-\partial_x(aF_z+bG_z)=a(\partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z)+b(\partial_zG_x-\partial_xG_z)$ and the third is $\partial_x(aF_y+bG_y)-\partial_y(aF_x+bG_x)=a(\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)+b(\partial_xG_y-\partial_yG_x)$. The three coordinates are those of $a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.3 By [F1], $\operatorname{div}(fF)=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i(fF_i)$, and step 1.1 rewrites each summand as $(\partial_if)F_i+f\,\partial_iF_i$. Splitting the sum gives $\sum_{i<n}(\partial_if)F_i+f\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, whose first term is $\langle\nabla f,F\rangle$ by [F2] and [F4] and whose second is $f\operatorname{div}F$ by [F1]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.4 By [F1], the first coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}(fF)$ is $\partial_y(fF_z)-\partial_z(fF_y)$, which step 1.1 rewrites as $\bigl((\partial_yf)F_z-(\partial_zf)F_y\bigr)+f(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y)$. By [F2] and [F3] with $u=\nabla f$ and $v=F$, the first bracket is the first coordinate $u_yv_z-u_zv_y$ of $\nabla f\times F$, and the second summand is $f$ times the first coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}F$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.5 By [F1], the second coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}(fF)$ is $\partial_z(fF_x)-\partial_x(fF_z)$, which step 1.1 rewrites as $\bigl((\partial_zf)F_x-(\partial_xf)F_z\bigr)+f(\partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z)$. By [F2] and [F3] the first bracket is the second coordinate $u_zv_x-u_xv_z$ of $\nabla f\times F$, and the second summand is $f$ times the second coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}F$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.6 By [F1], the third coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}(fF)$ is $\partial_x(fF_y)-\partial_y(fF_x)$, which step 1.1 rewrites as $\bigl((\partial_xf)F_y-(\partial_yf)F_x\bigr)+f(\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$. By [F2] and [F3] the first bracket is the third coordinate $u_xv_y-u_yv_x$ of $\nabla f\times F$, and the second summand is $f$ times the third coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}F$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Steps 2.4, 2.5 and 2.6 give the three coordinates of $\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F$, so $\operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F$; with steps 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 this is every assertion of the Statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 2.5, step 2.6] ∎

## Remarks

- **The scalar $f$ need only be $C^1$.** No mixed second derivative of $f$ appears in either product rule, so nothing here needs $C^2$; the identities of [[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]] and [[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]] are where the second-order hypothesis becomes necessary.

snapshot.title: Existence and uniqueness for the smooth exterior vector Helmholtz mixed boundary problem
snapshot.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the explicitly used variational, Sobolev and compact-spectral suppliers (and, for the exterior branch, the Fredholm alternative). Let $O\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set with $C^\infty$ boundary, let $D=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline O$ be connected, let $k>0$, and let $R>0$ with $\overline O\subset B_R(0)$. For every smooth tangent field $e_T$ on $\partial O$ there is exactly one field $E$, $C^\infty$ on $\overline D$, satisfying, with the Euclidean Laplacian acting componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]),
$$(\Delta+k^2)E=0\ \text{ on }D,\qquad \operatorname{div}E=0\ \text{ on }D,\qquad E_{\text{tangential}}=e_T\ \text{ on }\partial O,$$
and outgoing on the large sphere $S_R$ in the modal sense of [[lem-em-sphere-outgoing-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]. Given the prescribed tangential trace and $\operatorname{div}E=0$, the corresponding normal closure is the relation $\partial_nE_n+(\operatorname{div}n)E_n=-\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T$ with $n$ the outward normal of the truncated exterior region $B_R\setminus\overline O$ (pointing into $O$ on the inner boundary). This is the explicit Maxwell boundary closure used by the PEC scattering consumer; three independent scalar Dirichlet data are not asserted to be equivalent.
snapshot.strategy:
Reduction to a coercive shifted form. On the truncated annulus $A=B_R\setminus\overline O$ introduce $X=\{v\in H^1(A;\mathbb C^3):v_{	ext{tangential}}=0	ext{ on }\partial O\}$, a closed subspace of $H^1$ by the trace continuity of [[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]]; the trace machinery is smooth for the classical solutions. With $\kappa=\operatorname{div}n$ on the inner boundary, the form
$$a(E,v)=\int_A igl(
abla E:\overline{
abla v}-k^2E\cdot\overline v igr)+\int_{\partial O}\kappa E_n\overline{v_n}-\langle T_RE,vangle_{S_R}$$
is bounded on $H^1$ by [[lem-em-sphere-outgoing-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]] and bounded $\kappa$. Its real part is coercive after shifting by a real $\lambda>k^2+C_\delta+1$: the outer term is nonnegative by the sign of $\operatorname{Re}T_R$, and the curvature term is absorbed by the collar inequality proved in [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] with $2ab\le\delta a^2+\delta^{-1}b^2$. The complex coercive form is inverted by the explicit contraction iteration (Hilbert Riesz representation [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] turns the shifted form into a bounded operator $B$ with $\operatorname{Re}\langle Bx,xangle\ge\alpha\|x\|^2$; for small $t>0$, $x\mapsto(I-tB)x+tf$ is a strict contraction in the complete space). The $L^2$ pairing $J:X	o X^*$ is compact because the argument of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] gives $X\hookrightarrow L^2$ compact on the smooth bounded domain $A$; the original form operator is a shifted inverse composed with $I-\lambda K$, $K$ compact, so the Fredholm alternative [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]] (with its Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]) gives bounded invertibility once the kernel is zero. Kernel. For a homogeneous solution the imaginary part of $a(E,E)$ is $-\operatorname{Im}\langle T_RE,Eangle=0$, and the strictly positive DtN imaginary coefficients force all three outer traces of $E$ to vanish. Extending the field by the outgoing series outside $B_R$ and integrating by parts with [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] gives a weak componentwise Helmholtz solution on $D$ with $H^1$ regularity on each bounded local patch, because the full traces agree across $S_R$, and it vanishes outside $B_R$. On each such patch apply [[thm-interior-h-two-regularity-for-divergence-form-equations]] with principal matrix $I$, $b=0$, $c=-k^2$, $f=0$ (equivalently $-\Delta E=k^2E$), giving $H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The real and imaginary parts of each component then satisfy $\Delta w=-k^2w$ on the connected $D$ and vanish on its nonempty exterior open subset, so the direct local supplier [[thm-bounded-potential-weak-unique-continuation-in-three-dimensions]] makes them zero. No scalar inner Dirichlet condition is inferred from tangential PEC data, and the scalar exterior-Dirichlet lemma is not invoked in this kernel step. Hence the kernel is zero and the shifted-then-unshifted problem is boundedly invertible. Inhomogeneous data. For prescribed smooth $e_T$, give each Cartesian scalar component the Dirichlet boundary datum $(e_T)_j$ on $\partial O$ and zero on $S_R$. The weak prescribed-trace solver [[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]] with principal coefficient $I$ and zero bulk source, followed by the scalar smooth-data upgrade [[lem-em-smooth-domain-elliptic-regularity]], supplies a smooth componentwise lift $G$ on $\overline A$ with $G|_{\partial O}=e_T$ and $G|_{S_R}=0$ (apply to real and imaginary parts). This is a genuine scalar use of B7, distinct from the inline vector mixed-boundary regularity proof. Now solve for $u\in X$ with $a(u,v)=-a(G,v)-\int_{\partial O}(\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T)\overline{v_n}$; $E=G+u$ then has the prescribed tangential trace, and testing against compactly supported interior fields gives the componentwise Helmholtz equation and the stated normal relation. Regularity. At the artificial sphere the matched traces and normal derivatives make the extended field a weak Helmholtz solution across $S_R$, so [[cor-smooth-data-give-smooth-interior-solutions]] applied on bounded local patches to the constant-coefficient operator $-\Delta-k^2$ makes the matched field smooth there; no boundary theorem is used at this artificial interior surface. At $\partial O$ rotate into a smooth frame with two tangential components and one normal component; the principal part becomes a uniformly elliptic scalar principal matrix times the identity with smooth lower-order coupling, and the boundary system (two Dirichlet components and one Robin component) is complementing: in the frozen half-space a decaying principal mode $e^{i\xi\cdot y-|\xi|t}a$ with $\xi
e0$ has $a_1=a_2=0$ and $-|\xi|a_3=0$, so all amplitudes vanish, while curvature and connection terms are lower order. Supply the vector boundary argument inline, rather than treating B7's scalar public statement as a vector theorem. After the smooth frame rotation and boundary flattening, tangential shifts preserve the two zero Dirichlet component traces, while the normal component has arbitrary admissible trace. Test with $-\delta_{-h}(\eta^2\delta_h u)$ componentwise. The scalar principal matrix times the identity gives the sum of three positive gradient squares; smooth coefficient and frame commutators are lower-order $L^2$ terms bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz and Young. The differenced Robin boundary term consists of the bounded Robin coefficient times the normal quotient trace square and its smooth coefficient commutator; the collar estimate $\|w\|_{L^2(\partial O)}^2\le\delta\|
abla w\|_2^2+C_\delta\|w\|_2^2$ absorbs the first term, and trace continuity and Young bound the commutator by the same gradient bound and known $H^1$ data. This gives uniform tangential quotient-gradient bounds. Riesz identifies all mixed second derivatives in $L^2$, and the corrected component equation recovers each normal second derivative using the uniformly positive normal principal coefficient. Iterate the tangential quotient argument with differentiated smooth data and coefficient/Robin commutators, and recover remaining normal orders from the component equations; a finite boundary cover gives all orders. Local Sobolev extension/embedding then gives classical smooth representatives. This is the actual inline mixed-boundary product-space proof obligation, with two Dirichlet components and one Robin component; it is not replaced by a scalar Dirichlet-regularity citation. Divergence. The scalar $q=\operatorname{div}E$ is a smooth Helmholtz solution on $D$; the divergence identity in a boundary frame turns the inner Robin relation into $q=0$ on $\partial O$, and the outgoing component series differentiates to an outgoing $q$; [[lem-em-exterior-outgoing-scalar-uniqueness]] then gives $q=0$ on $D$. Thus $\operatorname{div}E=0$ is deduced, not presumed.

snapshot.title: Exact Helmholtz boundary representation with actual traces
snapshot.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded C-infinity domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let k>0 and x in Omega, and use the outgoing kernel $G_k$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. A sufficient classical specialization is that u and f extend smoothly to an open neighbourhood of the closed domain and $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ there. More generally, retain the justified weaker classical-trace branch: u is C2 inside Omega, u and all first derivatives extend continuously to its closure, f=(-Delta-k²)u belongs to L1(Omega), and the equation holds inside. The boundary values and normal derivative in the formula below are these actual continuous traces. Then
$$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)\,dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl[G_k(x-y)\partial_nu(y)-u(y)\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\bigr]dS_y,$$
with n the outward domain normal; both integrals are absolutely convergent. Merely being smooth on the OPEN domain without these trace/integrability data is insufficient.

For an exterior D=R3 minus closure of a bounded smooth obstacle, retain the exterior counterpart with actual inner boundary traces: suppose u is C2 on D with u and first derivatives continuous to its compact boundary, solves (-Delta-k²)u=f there, f is locally continuous and $\int_D|G_k(x-y)f(y)|dy$ is finite at the observation x, and the prescribed outgoing condition gives, uniformly on spheres at infinity, $u(y)=O(|y|^{-1})$ and $\partial_ru(y)-iku(y)=o(|y|^{-1})$. Then the same formula holds with volume D and its obstacle boundary, with n outward from D (pointing into the obstacle). Compactly supported L1 sources with the displayed local regularity are a sufficient source subclass. For the smooth-trace modal outgoing specialization beyond a source-containing sphere of radius $R_0>0$, retain the declared full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for this sufficient branch. Write the smooth angular trace as $g(n)=u(R_0n)$, use the real unit-sphere harmonics of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], set $c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}g(n)Y_{lm}(n)d\Omega(n)$, and define the outgoing modal class outside that sphere by
$$u(rn)=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}c_{lm}\,\frac{h_l(kr)}{h_l(kR_0)}Y_{lm}(n),\qquad r\ge R_0,$$
where $h_l$ are exactly the earlier explicit functions of [[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]. The proof below establishes smooth convergence, the homogeneous exterior equation, the actual trace g, the uniform bound $\sup_{r\ge R_0,n\in S^2}r|u(rn)|<\infty$ and the uniform Sommerfeld residual $\sup_{n\in S^2}r|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\to0$. Thus this existing smooth modal branch satisfies the prescribed far conditions without a later same-page supplier. Its full-Choice premise is retained; the earlier prescribed-outgoing branch remains under Countable Choice.

The Green formula uses the consistent actual pair of traces. Assigning both aperture values independently does not establish an exact boundary problem; a declared scalar aperture-source model remains a separate approximation. No weak boundary trace or normal trace for arbitrary rough data is asserted by mere interior smoothness.
snapshot.strategy:
For the closure-smooth bounded specialization, apply [[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] on Omega with a small ball about x removed. The k² terms cancel, the outgoing kernel's unit inner flux gives u(x), and its derivative-test term is O(delta); the source integral near x is finite since f is continuous there and G_k is locally integrable. This proves the stated signs.

For the weaker C2-interior/C1-closure trace branch, let S be the compact smooth boundary with its outward normal n. The exact [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]] under Countable Choice gives a normal tube with positive smooth radius; compactness gives a positive minimum. For sufficiently small t>0, $S_t=\{p-t n(p):p\in S\}$ lies inside Omega and bounds the inner domain Omega_t. In the normal graph charts the surface Jacobian and outward normals converge uniformly to those on S (the differential of p to p-tn(p) tends uniformly to the tangent identity). The one-sided graph convention makes this the actual inside collar; injectivity of the tube prevents overlap. For small t, x and a fixed ball about x lie in Omega_t. On each punctured Omega_t the ordinary Green theorem applies, since u is C2 on a neighbourhood of its compact closure. First remove the x-excision radius by the same local flux argument. Then take t down0: u and its gradient converge uniformly on S_t to their continuous actual traces, while G_k and its y-gradient are bounded and smooth on this collar away from x. The boundary integrals therefore converge to exactly the displayed trace integrals using the compact surface chart formula and the uniformly converging Jacobians. For the volume term, split off a small ball about x, where f is bounded and the kernel is integrable; on its complement G_k is bounded and f is L1. This gives an absolute integrable majorant, so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] on the increasing inner domains yields the full volume integral. This proves the weaker branch completely rather than assuming unspecified traces.

For the exterior branch, truncate by B_R and use the same inner-boundary trace limit and x-excision argument, with the outward obstacle normal pointing into the obstacle. For fixed observation x, on y=Rn the explicit kernel has $G_k(x-y)=O(R^{-1})$ and $\partial_R G_k(x-y)-ikG_k(x-y)=O(R^{-2})$, uniformly in n; these follow by differentiating the norm and $\partial_R|Rn-x|=1+O(R^{-2})$. In the outer Wronskian, write $G_k(\partial_Ru-iku)-u(\partial_RG_k-ikG_k)$: its supremum is o(R^-2)+O(R^-3), so multiplying by the sphere area O(R²) makes it tend to0. Absolute convergence of the stated volume integral then permits the limit R to infinity. The smooth-trace modal outgoing subclass has the explicit earlier-supplier proof below; its existing full-Choice sufficient premise is retained. Other prescribed uniform-outgoing data use only Countable Choice through Green, tubular and surface interfaces. No independent assignment of both boundary traces or unproved rough-trace Green theorem is used. The cited Green theorem has real inputs; apply it to the four real/imaginary component pairs and combine by complex bilinearity to obtain the displayed complex kernel identity, with no conjugation introduced.

Smooth angular coefficient estimate from finite angular calculus. For smooth w on S2 let $L_jw(n)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}w(Q_j(t)n)\right|_{t=0}$, where $Q_j(t)$ is the elementary coordinate rotation about e_j, and put $\Lambda=\sum_{j=1}^3L_j^2$. Its tangent velocity is $e_j\times n$ with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Rotation invariance of surface measure is the exact earlier [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]. Differentiate the invariant integral of w(Q_j(t)n)v(Q_j(t)n) on the compact sphere: uniform difference quotients of its smooth integrand give $\int(L_jw)v=-\int w(L_jv)$, so Lambda is symmetric under the bilinear integral; for complex data apply the same finite identity to components. No polar-operator theorem is presumed. On an ambient smooth extension, direct coordinate differentiation gives
$$\sum_jL_j^2=|x|^2\Delta-(x\cdot\nabla)^2-x\cdot\nabla.$$
Each Y_lm is the restriction of a degree-l homogeneous harmonic polynomial by the earlier H2 supplier, so Euler's identity and this finite formula give $\Lambda Y_{lm}=-l(l+1)Y_{lm}$. Therefore, for l>=1 and any integer p>=1, repeated symmetry and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] yield
$$[l(l+1)]^p c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}(-\Lambda)^pg\,Y_{lm}\,d\Omega,\qquad |c_{lm}|\le\frac{\|\Lambda^pg\|_2}{[l(l+1)]^p}.$$
The smooth g and all these angular derivatives are bounded on the compact sphere and have finite L2 norms. Treat l0 separately as its single finite constant coefficient. The addition diagonal of H2 gives $\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}$. With p2, the total weighted absolute sum
$$\sum_{l,m}(l+1+2kR_0)|c_{lm}|\,\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty<\infty$$
follows: for l>=1 its degree-l bound is a fixed constant times $(2l+1)(l+1+2kR_0)\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}[l(l+1)]^{-2}=O(l^{-3/2})$. This is the actual summability argument for every smooth trace, not an unproved claim of coefficient decay.

Exact radial majorants. From the earlier Hankel proof, $F_l(z)=z^2|h_l(z)|^2=\sum_{j=0}^la_jz^{-2j}$ has a0=1 and positive a_j, so it is nonincreasing in z>0. Consequently, for $\phi_l(r)=h_l(kr)/h_l(kR_0)$,
$$|\phi_l(r)|\le R_0/r\quad(r\ge R_0).$$
The same earlier supplier's exact t_l bounds, applied with radius r, give $|k h_l'(kr)/h_l(kr)|\le(l+1)/r+k$, hence
$$r|\phi_l'(r)-ik\phi_l(r)|\le R_0[(l+1)/r+2k]\le l+1+2kR_0.$$
For every FIXED l the explicit finite outgoing polynomial gives $r(\phi_l'-ik\phi_l)\to0$ as r tends infinity. The weighted coefficient sum therefore bounds every residual tail uniformly for ALL r>=R0 and n on the sphere. Given epsilon, choose a finite degree cutoff making that tail smaller than epsilon/2; the finitely many remaining radial residuals tend to0 uniformly after multiplication by their fixed finite angular suprema. This finite-head/finite-tail argument proves the uniform Sommerfeld limit. Also $r|u(rn)|\le R_0\sum|c_{lm}|\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty$ uniformly, which proves exactly the amplitude bound used in the outer Green Wronskian. The first radial derivative series is uniformly convergent on r>=R0 since $|\phi_l'|\le[(l+1)/R_0+k]|\phi_l|$ and the same weighted sum dominates it; finite-coordinate FTC [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]] identifies that derivative with partial_r u.

Smooth modal realization and normalization. Rotational differentiation preserves the degree-l harmonic space. Skew symmetry gives $\sum_j\|L_jv\|_2^2=l(l+1)\|v\|_2^2$ in that finite space, so each successive angular derivative has norm at most [l(l+1)]^(1/2) times the preceding norm. Its pointwise norm is bounded by sqrt((2l+1)/(4pi)) times its L2 norm by finite basis Cauchy-Schwarz and the addition identity. The radial ODE of the earlier Hankel supplier, differentiated finitely many times, gives for every fixed q a bound $|\phi_l^{(q)}(r)|\le C_{q,k,R_0}(l+1)^{2q}/r$ on r>=R0: q0 is the radial-ratio bound, q1 is the logarithmic-derivative bound, and the equation plus derivatives of r^-1,r^-2 gives the induction. Thus every radial/angular derivative series is dominated by a finite power of l times the coefficient estimate with a sufficiently large p. It converges uniformly on each closed bounded exterior annulus; FTC identifies all derivatives. Cartesian derivatives there are finite combinations of radial and angular derivatives with smooth coefficients (from $\nabla=n\partial_r-r^{-1}n\times(L_1,L_2,L_3)$), so the series defines a smooth exterior field. The finite angular identity above gives the polar Laplacian formula on phi_l(r)Y_lm, and the radial ODE makes each term solve (Delta+k²)u0; termwise second derivatives prove the equation for the limit. At rR0 the absolute series has its L2 coefficients c_lm; completeness of H2 and continuity give its actual smooth trace g. If trace coefficients are recorded instead in the sphere-normalized basis $Y^{R_0}_{lm}(R_0n)=R_0^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$, their coefficients are R0 c_lm, so the displayed expansion is identical after normalization. No weaker rough-trace claim or obstacle-boundary existence is inferred. All bounded Green, weaker C1-trace, exterior source and smooth-modal conclusions are preserved, with the same declared Choice strengths.

snapshot.title: Outgoing source Helmholtz field: fundamental solution, Fraunhofer and Fresnel error terms
snapshot.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. For $k>0$ define $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ off the origin, a locally integrable complex function. Then $$(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$$ distributionally. For a finite complex measure $\alpha$ supported in $B_a(0)$, the field $u=G_k*\alpha$ is smooth outside the support, solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there and is outgoing: for $x=rn$, $r\ge2a$, $$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$ uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. For a planar aperture $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ with observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$, $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, $a+b\ll z$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$ and relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$, hence absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. Aperture data are an explicitly specified scalar source, not asserted to be the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces, and no uniqueness or existence for arbitrary obstacle boundary data is claimed.
snapshot.strategy: For radial $f(r)$ one has $\Delta f=f''+2f'/r$ by direct coordinate differentiation of $\partial_ir=x_i/r$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), and inserting $f=G_k$ gives $(\Delta+k^2)f=0$ for $r>0$. For the distributional identity excise a ball $B_\delta$ inside a compact test integration; the second Green identity ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) on the excised domain cancels the $k^2$ terms and leaves the inner flux, where $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1)$: the derivative-test boundary term is $O(\delta)$ and the leading unit flux multiplies $\psi(0)$, while the local $k^2G_k$ integral is $O(\delta^2)$; the limit is $\delta_0$ with the displayed sign. Off-support smoothness and all derivatives follow from the positive separation of compact observation and source sets, with differentiation under the source integral. For the Fraunhofer error write $R=|rn-y|$ and use the norm expansion of the cited dipole-remainder technique ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]): $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le Ca^2/r$ and $|r/R-1|\le Ca/r$; the exponential difference is bounded by $C r^{-1}(a/r+ka^2/r)$ via $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$, and integrating against the total variation of $\alpha$ with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) gives the displayed error; the outgoing relation follows from $\partial_rR=1+O(a^2/r^2)$ and $R^{-2}=O(r^{-2})$. The Fresnel estimate is the Taylor expansion of the norm with explicit remainder on the compact small-$s$ region $s=|\xi-y|^2/z^2$, using $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$. Countable Choice is inherited by the actually used Green, surface/regular-distribution and/or harmonic-boundary supplier interfaces. The supplier updates do not alter the local source, trace or modal class used here. To make the cited norm-remainder TECHNIQUE an actual calculation, for h(s)=|x-sy| one has $h'(0)=-n\cdot y$ and $h''(s)=|y|^2/|x-sy|-((x-sy)\cdot y)^2/|x-sy|^3$, whose modulus is at most $2a^2/(r-a)$ when |y|<=a and r>=2a. The finite Riemann FTC remainder therefore gives |R-r+n dot y|<=Ca²/r; the same lower bound yields |r/R-1|<=Ca/r. Thus this is proved directly, not falsely deduced from a supplier statement about the inverse kernel integral. For integration against a finite COMPLEX measure alpha, the estimate |integral h d alpha|<=sup|h| times ||alpha||TV follows first for finite simple functions from the defining total variation, then for bounded continuous kernels by uniform finite-simple approximation of their range. Every off-support parameter derivative is continuous and uniformly bounded on compact observation/source products, so uniform difference quotients through this finite-measure bound prove all derivatives without an unprovided complex-measure dominated-convergence premise. Finally $\partial_r R=1+O(a²/r²)$ in the explicit radial derivative formula gives the claimed outgoing O(r^-1) estimate after multiplication by r. For the Fresnel remainder, write s=|xi-y|²/z²; on any prescribed small-angle range (a+b)/z<=eta0<1, twice-FTC gives |sqrt(1+s)-1-s/2|<=s²/8 and |(1+s)^(-1/2)-1|<=s/2. Combined with |exp(i theta)-1|<=|theta| these yield exactly the original phase, relative amplitude and absolute field error bounds, uniformly on that declared range. The finite-total-variation branch and every original exterior/approximation claim are retained.

snapshot.title: Period averages of products of real parts of complex exponentials
snapshot.statement: Let $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, and let $a,d\in\mathbb C$ (or $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, componentwise). Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d),$$ and the dot-product and cross-product versions hold componentwise. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation.
snapshot.strategy: Write $\operatorname{Re}(z)=(z+\overline z)/2$; the product is one constant term $\frac14(a\overline d+\overline ad)$ plus oscillatory terms $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$, which integrate to zero over a full period by the fundamental theorem applied to $e^{\pm2i\omega t}/(\pm2i\omega)$.

snapshot.statement: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, $c>0$ and $\omega>0$, and let $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$. Define $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by $E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the classes). Then: (a) [Calculus] if $\widetilde E,\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, then $E,B$ are $C^1$ and at every $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$: $\partial_tE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; for each $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\partial_jE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\partial_j\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; and with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] acting on the spatial variable, $\operatorname{div}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{div}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, $\operatorname{curl}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$. (b) [Injectivity] if $w\in\mathbb C^3$ and $\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, then $w=0$; more generally, if $w:D\to\mathbb C^3$ is continuous and $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$, then $w\equiv0$ on $D$. (c) [Equivalence] if $\widetilde E,\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, the phasor system $$\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=0,\quad\operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B,\quad\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E$$ holds on $D$ if and only if the real system $$\operatorname{div}E=0,\quad\operatorname{div}B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\quad\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$$ holds on $D\times\mathbb R$.
snapshot.strategy: Write the encoding in real components: by the Cartesian form and Euler identity of [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=(\operatorname{Re}w(x))\cos(\omega t)+(\operatorname{Im}w(x))\sin(\omega t)$ componentwise, with the real and imaginary parts of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and the complex arithmetic of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. (a) For fixed $x$ each component is a constant-coefficient combination of $\cos(\omega t)$ and $\sin(\omega t)$; the affine map $t\mapsto\omega t$ has derivative $\omega$ by [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], and [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] applied to the differentiable real sine and cosine maps of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] gives their composite derivatives. The sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] then give $\partial_tE=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde Ee^{-i\omega t})$, and the spatial derivatives pass through the constant coefficients, giving the spatial formulas for each component; the divergence and curl formulas follow by applying the componentwise formulas and the linearity of [[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]] (for complex fields, componentwise in real and imaginary parts). (b) Evaluating at $t=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$; evaluating at $t=\pi/(2\omega)$ gives $\operatorname{Re}(-iw)=\operatorname{Im}w=0$ by the quarter-turn values of [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]] and the Cartesian form of [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], so $w=0$. The continuous case applies the pointwise result at each $x\in D$; no choice principle is used. (c) Direction (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): substitute the phasor equations into the calculus formulas of (a); e.g. $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(i\omega\widetilde Be^{-i\omega t})=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde Ee^{-i\omega t})=c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Direction (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): subtract the complex expressions and apply (b), e.g. $\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E-i\omega\widetilde B)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)$ forces $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B$; the other three equations are analogous. All statements are pointwise algebraic identities; no PDE existence, no boundary condition and no choice principle is used.

      url: "https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_rirect.html"

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Darboux and tagged Riemann integrability agree, with the same value ([[thm-multidimensional-darboux-equals-riemann]]).

[F2] Under Countable Choice, any set between the interior and closure of a box has its box volume as Lebesgue measure ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F3] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous and agrees with the simple integral on nonnegative simple functions ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F4] Lebesgue integration is complex-linear on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F5] Assume [[def-countable-choice]], used for F2 and the Lebesgue-measure interface.

[F6] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]), and a compact subset of a metric space is closed ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]). Riemann integration over a bounded Jordan set is defined by the zero extension to a bounding rectangle ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]), and a continuous real function on a compact Jordan set is integrable in that sense ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]).

## Proof

**Given:** the bounded Borel Riemann integrand and F5.

1.1 Choose $C\ge0$ with $|f|\le C$, and put $g=f+C\ge0$. F2 and F3 give $\int_Q|f|\le C\operatorname{vol}Q<\infty$ and $\int_Qg\le2C\operatorname{vol}Q<\infty$, so both are integrable. Borel measurability makes all these integrals defined. [given, F2, F3, F5]

2.1 For a finite rectangular grid, list its closed cells $Q_1,\ldots,Q_s$ and set $D_i=Q_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}Q_j$. These Borel sets partition $Q$, contain each cell's interior and lie in its closure, so $\lambda_n(D_i)=\operatorname{vol}Q_i$ by F2. Put $m_i=\inf_{Q_i}g$ and $M_i=\sup_{Q_i}g$. The simple functions $l=\sum_i m_i\mathbf1_{D_i}$ and $h=\sum_i M_i\mathbf1_{D_i}$ satisfy $l\le g\le h$ everywhere, including grid faces. F3 identifies their integrals as the grid's lower and upper Darboux sums for $g$, so these sums bracket $\int_Qg$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 Every tagged sum of $g$ is the corresponding sum of $f$ plus $C\operatorname{vol}Q$. Thus $g$ is Riemann integrable with value $I_R(f)+C\operatorname{vol}Q$. F1 says its supremum of lower Darboux sums and infimum of upper sums have this same value. Taking these bounds in step 2.1 squeezes $\int_Qg$ to that value. F4 and F2 then give $\int_Qf=\int_Qg-C\operatorname{vol}Q=I_R(f)$. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F4]

4.1 Apply the real result separately to the real and imaginary parts for the complex assertion; the bound $|f|\le|\operatorname{Re}f|+|\operatorname{Im}f|$ ensures absolute integrability. For the last clause, let $E\subseteq Q$ be compact Jordan and let $h:E\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. If $E$ is empty its zero extension is zero. Otherwise F6 makes $h$ bounded, and compactness makes $E$ closed. Its zero extension $\widetilde h$ is Borel: for every open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$, continuity in the subspace gives $h^{-1}(O)=E\cap G$ for some open $G\subseteq Q$; then $\widetilde h^{-1}(O)=E\cap G$ when $0\notin O$, while $\widetilde h^{-1}(O)=(Q\setminus E)\cup(E\cap G)$ when $0\in O$. The definition and theorem in F6 say exactly that this bounded zero extension is Riemann integrable on $Q$. The real result therefore applies; treating real and imaginary parts gives the same conclusion for continuous complex integrands, in particular smooth compact test integrands. The zero function has both integrals zero; the constant one has both integrals $\operatorname{vol}Q$. Degenerate boxes are excluded from this statement. No choices of tags over an infinite family were used; Countable Choice is precisely the measure hypothesis in F2. $\square$ [step 3.1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6]

snapshot.title: Declared material-closure branches: linear nondispersive Ohmic response and the causal memory branch
snapshot.statement:
Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].
(a) [Material rest frame] The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in which the material element under consideration is at rest, with spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; when the material is at rest in the laboratory frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the components below are the laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.
(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch] In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes $$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$ where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$; local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.
(c) [Causal memory branch] Alternatively, and again in the rest frame, the polarisation response to the electric history is the causal convolution $$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$ for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]); the integral then converges absolutely for bounded continuous histories $E$ because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The kernel class actually used, together with causality and passivity, is part of the model and is analysed in [[pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response]]; neither causality nor passivity is automatic. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).
(d) [Status] These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.
snapshot.strategy: An adopted nonproof formulation. The objects are those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]; the macroscopic field equations whose formulation the closure completes are those of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; the rest-frame notion is the inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] used by [[def-em-lab-geometry]], and the memory-branch kernel class is the $L^1$ notion of [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], whose absolute convergence for bounded continuous histories is the elementary domination displayed in the statement. The finitely-subtracted branch uses the holomorphy notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]] and states its growth and boundary hypotheses explicitly rather than hiding them. Clause (d) records that the branches are assumptions with no microscopic or empirical content. No proof is supplied and none is claimed, in accordance with the nonproof status of a postulate; the source and scope review covers the formulation, the rest-frame and scale qualifications and the non-derivation.

snapshot.title: Adopted scalar aperture-diffraction model (polarization-insensitive regime)
snapshot.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the smooth modal full-Choice branch of the latter is not used. Adopt as a model assumption of the framework the following scalar aperture-diffraction model. [Data] Fix an angular frequency $\omega>0$ and wavenumber $k:=\omega/c$, with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $S\subset\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$ be a nonempty compact subset of a declared aperture plane $y_3=0$ with aperture radius $a>0$ (the screening plane and spatial region are read in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]), and let $\alpha$ be a finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^3$ supported in $S$ (the **aperture distribution**), with $\alpha$ read in volts so that the model field below carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ of an electric-field component and its pairings are those of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. [Model field] The model assigns to every observation point $x$ with $x_3>0$ the complex scalar amplitude $$u(x):=\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y),$$ where $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ is the outgoing Helmholtz kernel of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], together with the real scalar field $U(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and the model period-averaged squared field $(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. All model predictions are declared comparisons of this squared field between observation points; no absolute radiometric power or intensity calibration is adopted. [Adopted regime and status] The model is the declared polarization-insensitive scalar approximation of aperture diffraction. It ignores the vector nature and polarization of the electromagnetic field, takes the aperture distribution rather than the exact screen traces as its datum, assigns no back-reaction of the diffracted field on the illumination and no screen interaction beyond the aperture, and is not derived from either branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] or from the material-closure branches of [[post-em-material-closure]]; it is a declared optical approximation, not an exact electromagnetic model. It does not assert that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and it does not identify $\alpha$ with the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces: assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, as recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]], and the error terms of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] are the controlled content of the model. No measured intensity, apparatus, sampling model, uncertainty budget, empirical comparison or quantitative radiometric calibration is adopted.
snapshot.strategy: This is an explicit adopted-assumption contract; it is deliberately not a derivation. (i) The mathematical object it adopts is the outgoing source field $u=G_k*\alpha$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], whose kernel and outgoing/Fraunhofer technique are fixed there. This model permits the compact closed-radius support $|y|\le a$, including aperture corners. Its integral and off-support regularity fall under that supplier by choosing any containing open ball of radius $A>a$; the sharp-radius estimates at $r\ge2a$ are proved directly in the consuming diffraction theorem, so this extension does not evaluate an open-support hypothesis at a boundary point; the integral against the finite complex measure is that of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. (ii) The physical reading uses the aperture plane and spatial region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the wavenumber-frequency relation $k=\omega/c$ and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (iii) The non-derivation clause is essential: neither the smooth nor the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] implies this scalar source model, and the finite-conductivity/material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]] contain no ideal aperture or screen model; the trace caveat is the one recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]]. (iv) The scope sentences exclude exact Maxwell, vector, polarization, back-reaction, absolute-radiometric and empirical content. The item uses no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited mathematical suppliers (the kernel lemma carries Countable Choice, as stated there). The Countable Choice hypothesis is inherited verbatim from the cited kernel and boundary-representation suppliers; this postulate adds no choice use of its own.
